entries.clue: Lose erection then no erection – be tolerant! (2,4,2)

indicatorNotes.erection: An erection is something raised upright, so in a down entry 'no' erected is written from the bottom up.

blocks.note: To go soft is to lose an erection.
NO stood on its end, read upwards.

annotation.surface: A frank piece of bedroom counselling urging a partner not to mind a flop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Erection' appears twice with two jobs: first it is plain anatomy, then it is the instruction to stand NO upright. In a down entry, raising a word means reading it upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: To go soft on someone is the idiom for being lenient or tolerant towards them.

entries.clue: It's public knowledge effectively, so pretence is bollocks (4,6)

indicatorNotes.is bollocks: Something that is bollocks, in British slang, is a mess or rubbish, so the letters are to be scrambled.

blocks.note: The ten letters of SO PRETENCE rearranged.

annotation.surface: A cynic dismissing a politician's pretence as nonsense because everyone already knows the truth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks' reads as a dismissive verdict, but here it is the scrambling instruction. The fodder is the ten letters immediately before it.
annotation.definitionFit: An open secret is something supposedly confidential that is in practice common knowledge, so it is public knowledge in effect.

entries.clue: Maybe 'X' has Blair squirming, trapped in state enquiry initially (8)

indicatorNotes.squirming: Squirming is wriggling out of shape, so BLAIR's letters twist into a new order.
indicatorNotes.trapped in: Trapped in means held inside, so the scrambled name sits within the state and the E.
indicatorNotes.initially: Initially points to the start of the word, taking only its opening letter.

blocks.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Virginia.
BLAIR's letters, squirming into a new order.
The first letter of enquiry.

annotation.surface: Tony Blair wriggling under questioning at a state inquiry, with a mysterious 'X' in the frame.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State enquiry' reads as a public inquiry of the kind Blair faced over Iraq, but it splits in two: 'state' is VA, and 'enquiry' gives only its initial E.
annotation.definitionFit: In algebra X is the classic name for a variable, the unknown quantity; 'Maybe' flags it as an example.

entries.clue: see 25ac. (4)
(& 9ac.) Brown, beset by several disapproving socialist leaders, gets depressed and resigns (6)

indicatorNotes.beset by: Beset by means surrounded by, so the brown sits inside the other letters.
indicatorNotes.leaders: Leaders are the ones at the front, so each word gives its first letter.

blocks.note: The leading letters of several, disapproving and socialist.
Tan is a light brown.
Someone depressed is down.

annotation.surface: Gordon Brown, surrounded by disapproving Labour grandees, sinking into gloom and quitting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brown' is dressed up as Gordon Brown, the former Labour leader, but it is only a colour. The initials come from the three words, not the socialist leaders in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand down is the usual phrase for giving up an office, which is what resigning means.

entries.clue: As a street interview very often starts with Times: drink (3,3)

indicatorNotes.starts: Starts are beginnings, so each of the two words gives its first letter.

blocks.note: The first letters of very and often.
X is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'.
Pop is a fizzy drink.

annotation.surface: A reporter noting that street interviews open with a question about drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign X. 'Very often' supplies only its two initials.
annotation.definitionFit: A vox pop, from Latin vox populi, 'voice of the people', is an informal interview with passers-by, and the phrase also works adjectivally.
annotation.definitionNote: 'As a street interview' reads adjectivally, and VOX POP is used attributively in just that way.

entries.clue: Bird seed sex (5)

blocks.note: A pip is a fruit seed.
IT is old slang for sex, or sex appeal.

annotation.surface: Three blunt words that could be a birdwatcher's note on the mating season.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bird seed' pairs itself as birdseed, but 'Bird' is the definition and 'seed' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A pipit is a small brown songbird of open country.

entries.clue: Ex-PM's disciple: prick securing bolthole (8)

indicatorNotes.securing: Securing means holding fast, so the prick holds the bolthole inside it.

blocks.note: A bite, from an insect, is a small prick in the skin.
A lair is an animal's hideout.

annotation.surface: A sneer at a Tony Blair loyalist as a prick who has found himself a safe hiding place.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prick' reads as an insult aimed at the disciple, but it is wordplay for a small wound. The Ex-PM is Tony Blair, Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007.
annotation.definitionFit: A Blairite is a follower of Tony Blair, the former Prime Minister.

entries.clue: (& 15dn.) Wears the trousers after skirt - a big factor in Ukip's campaign (6)

annotation.definition: a big factor in Ukip's campaign

indicatorNotes.after: After means following, so the trouser-wearing word comes second, behind the skirt.

blocks.note: To skirt something is to border it.
Whoever wears the trousers controls the household.

annotation.surface: A dig at Ukip's campaign as a story of men asserting themselves over women in skirts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Skirt' and 'trousers' conjure clothing and gender roles, but 'skirt' is a verb here. Ukip, the UK Independence Party, campaigned hard on immigration.
annotation.definitionFit: Border controls, checks on who may enter the country, were the centre of Ukip's 2015 immigration pitch.

entries.clue: see 5dn. (4)
MPs, altogether a primal shambles and little fun (10)

indicatorNotes.shambles: A shambles is a chaotic mess, so the letters beside it are thrown into disorder.
indicatorNotes.little: Little asks for the short form, so fun becomes its abbreviation.

blocks.note: Seven letters for the shambles.
ENT is short for entertainment.

annotation.surface: A jaundiced view of the Commons as a primitive, joyless mess.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shambles' is the anagram indicator, but it also sums up the surface verdict on MPs. The ENT joins the letters before they are scrambled.
annotation.definitionFit: Parliament is the body of MPs taken all together.

entries.clue: Luvvies here tense with passion before Brenda's comeback (7)

indicatorNotes.before: Before places what precedes it ahead of what follows.
indicatorNotes.comeback: A comeback is a return, so the Queen's letters run back the other way.

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense.
Heat is intensity of feeling.
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, ER, reversed here.

annotation.surface: Overwrought actors on edge before a royal return to the stage.
annotation.walkthrough: Private Eye readers know the Queen as 'Brenda', so 'Brenda's' stands for ER, Elizabeth Regina.
annotation.definitionFit: Luvvies is British slang for gushing actors, and the theatre is where they are found.

entries.clue: Bums screwing around with amphetamines put into confusion (6)

indicatorNotes.screwing around: Screwing around means twisting about, so the letters are turned into a new order.

blocks.note: The word itself, for scrambling.
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, an amphetamine-type drug, and more than one gives two Es.

annotation.surface: Layabouts sleeping around on speed and ending up baffled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Screwing around' reads as promiscuity but is the anagram signal. The plural 'amphetamines' supplies two Es.
annotation.definitionFit: To bemuse is to bewilder, putting someone into confusion.

entries.clue: 'Labour success confers such status' – Archer's old lady? (10)

blocks.note: Old lady is slang for one's mother.
The Archer is Robin Hood.

annotation.surface: A Labour slogan attributed to Mary Archer, wife of the novelist and Tory peer Jeffrey Archer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Labour' is childbirth, not the party. 'Archer's old lady' suggests Jeffrey Archer's wife, but it's Robin Hood's mother, Mother Hood.
annotation.definitionFit: A successful labour produces a baby and so makes the woman a mother, conferring motherhood.

entries.clue: Ecclesiastical "fire"? Get out of the habit (7)

blocks.note: To sack a priest.
To take off a frock, the monk's habit.

annotation.surface: A church sacking framed as someone kicking a bad habit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Habit' pretends to mean a routine, but it is the robe. Taking the robe off is exactly what unfrocking means.
annotation.definitionFit: To unfrock a cleric is to strip him of priestly office, which is the church's firing, and literally to take off his frock or habit.

entries.clue: see 8dn. (8)
Like a more traditional Socialist took off his motley (7)

indicatorNotes.motley: Motley means jumbled and multicoloured, so the letters of 'his' come out mixed.

blocks.note: To take off is to leave, past tense LEFT.
HIS rearranged.

annotation.surface: An old-school socialist stripping off his jester's costume.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Took off his motley' reads as undressing, since motley is the jester's costume, but it splits into LEFT and a jumble of HIS.
annotation.definitionFit: Leftish means somewhat left-wing, the leaning of old-style socialists as opposed to New Labour.

entries.clue: Miliband? "I'm in broadcast!", which is the dregs (8)

indicatorNotes.in: In places the preceding words inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: A broadcast is sent out.
Ed Miliband, Labour leader until 2015.
The word itself, apostrophe dropped.

annotation.surface: Ed Miliband boasting that he's on air, with a verdict that he is the lowest of the low.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Miliband' stands for his first name alone, a common trick with politicians. The quoted boast is not speech but two pieces placed inside a word for 'broadcast'.
annotation.definitionFit: Sediment is the matter that settles at the bottom of a liquid, the dregs.

entries.clue: Excited state in parliament is wasted (6)

indicatorNotes.in: In says the answer lies inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: Running across parliamenT IS WASted.

annotation.surface: A jibe that an agitated Parliament is a waste of everyone's time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' reads as the definition, meaning drunk, which pulls towards a word for tipsy. The answer hides across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A tizwas or tiswas is British slang for a state of excited confusion, as in 'all of a tiswas'.

entries.clue: Smear working precisely (4-2)

blocks.note: A spot is a mark or smear.
A machine that is on is working.

annotation.surface: A smear campaign that hits its target exactly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smear' suggests the political kind, but it is a plain blot. 'On' for 'working' is a standard crossword equivalence.
annotation.definitionFit: Spot-on is British informal for exactly right, precisely.
annotation.definitionNote: Spot-on usually works as an adjective, but it is also used adverbially ('she judged it spot-on'), matching 'precisely'.

entries.clue: Fair following for Penny's hole (6)

indicatorNotes.for: For means in place of, so the penny takes the following letter's spot.

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in 'p. 3f'; it is the letter swapped out.
P is the abbreviation for a penny, and it goes in where the F was.
Fair hair or skin is light.

annotation.surface: A crude joke about a woman named Penny and a body part.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penny's hole' is the smut, but the 's is 'is' and 'hole' is the definition. F plus LIGHT makes FLIGHT before the P swaps in.
annotation.definitionFit: Being 'in a hole' is the idiom for being stuck in difficulties, and a plight is exactly that kind of dangerous or awkward situation.

entries.clue: After one bender, screwed as hillbillies stereotypically do? (7)

indicatorNotes.screwed: Screwed means twisted, so the letters are wrenched into a new order.

blocks.note: The Roman numeral for one.
The word itself, for twisting.

annotation.surface: A hillbilly's drunken night ending in bed with a relative.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bender' reads as a drinking spree and 'screwed' as sex, but 'bender' is the fodder and 'screwed' the twist.
annotation.definitionFit: Inbreeding, mating within a close family, is the stereotype pinned on isolated hillbilly communities; the question mark flags the definition by example.

entries.clue: More than one party generates bollocks (5)

blocks.note: Formal dances, in the plural.
British slang for nonsense, and for testicles.

annotation.surface: A cynic's view that multi-party politics produces only rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' pushes towards politics after a clue full of MPs, but it's the social kind.
annotation.definitionFit: A ball is a grand dance party, so several are balls; balls and bollocks are both British slang for testicles and for nonsense.

entries.clue: Retirement means coitus interruptus? (10)

blocks.note: Retiring from a scene is withdrawing.
The contraceptive method of pulling out.

annotation.surface: A crude gag that retiring from politics amounts to pulling out early.
annotation.walkthrough: Retreat and pulling out are the same word. The question mark admits the second sense is a cheeky example.
annotation.definitionFit: Withdrawal is retirement from a place or position, and also the everyday name for coitus interruptus as a birth-control method.

entries.clue: see 25ac. (4)
(&4dn./24dn.) Comfortable place for battered Miliband, initially dividing the Houses (4)

indicatorNotes.battered: Battered means knocked out of shape, so the letters of 'for' are rearranged.
indicatorNotes.initially: Initially takes the opening letter of the name before it.
indicatorNotes.dividing: Dividing means coming between, so the new letters sit between two HOMEs.

blocks.note: Two houses, each a HOME, split to take the insert.
FOR, battered into a new order.
The first letter of Miliband.

annotation.surface: Ed Miliband, beaten in the 2015 election, looking for somewhere soft to land between the Houses of Parliament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word but is the anagram fodder. 'The Houses' suggests Parliament, yet here it just means two homes.
annotation.definitionFit: A home from home is a place where you feel as comfortable as in your own house.

entries.clue: Cock-up quiet promenades (8)

blocks.note: SH is the call for quiet.
To promenade is to amble at leisure.

annotation.surface: A botched, hushed-up stroll along the seafront.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Promenades' looks like a noun, seaside walkways, but it is the verb, strolls, matching AMBLES.
annotation.definitionFit: A cock-up is British slang for a mess or blunder, which is a shambles.

entries.clue: Makes love like an old-timer, putting penis head in shortly before beginning to shrink (6)

indicatorNotes.head: The head of a word is its front, so penis gives its first letter.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts that letter inside the next word.
indicatorNotes.before: Before puts that word ahead of the letter that follows.
indicatorNotes.beginning: The beginning of a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: The head, the first letter, of penis.
Shortly means soon.
The first letter of shrink; 'to' just joins it.

annotation.surface: An elderly lover's performance described with anatomical frankness, ending in shrinkage.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is anatomical, but 'head' and 'beginning' each take one first letter. SOON is split by the P and then gets an S tacked on.
annotation.definitionFit: To spoon is old-fashioned slang for courting and canoodling, so it is lovemaking as an old-timer would put it.
